standard.title: Generate, modify and evaluate designs
standard.description: Generate, modify, communicate and evaluate designs
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can generate, communicate and compare designs (AC9TDI4P03). They have produced and communicated design ideas and made comparisons. They have not yet formally evaluated designs against criteria or made and documented modifications to a preferred design based on evaluation.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students generate a range of design ideas, evaluate them against design criteria and user stories, select a preferred design, and modify it where it does not satisfy all criteria.

nodes.label: Generating a range of design ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can generate multiple distinct design ideas for a given problem rather than pursuing the first idea
nodes.minimum_width: Generate at least two design ideas for the same problem that are genuinely different (not minor variations)
nodes.typical_width: Ideate a range of possible design solutions; represent each idea clearly enough that it can be compared to others; produce sketches, diagrams or descriptions for each
wider: Use a structured ideation method (e.g. sketching six thumbnails, mind-mapping from the user story) to generate ideas beyond the first obvious solution

Generate design ideas that each prioritise a different design criterion — e.g. one idea optimises for cost, another for accessibility, another for ease of use — making trade-offs explicit from the start

response_modes.reason: Students who default to their first idea lack ideation repertoire — they do not know how to generate alternatives. Accumulated experience with ideation methods (thumbnail sketches, constraint-flipping, stakeholder-first framing) builds the repertoire needed for genuine comparison.

success_criteria: Produces at least two design ideas that are meaningfully different
Each idea is represented clearly enough to be compared
nodes.hinge_reason: Genuine ideation in N1 is a prerequisite for evaluation in N2 — if students produce only one idea or near-identical variations, N2's comparative evaluation against criteria collapses into description. The evaluate step requires at least two meaningfully different options.

nodes.label: Evaluating designs against criteria and user stories
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate design ideas against design criteria and user stories and identify which idea best meets them
nodes.minimum_width: Compare at least two design ideas against the design criteria and user stories; state which idea better satisfies them and give at least one reason
nodes.typical_width: Use the design criteria to systematically evaluate each idea (e.g. rate each against each criterion); identify a preferred design and explain which criteria it best satisfies and where it falls short
wider: Use a weighted decision matrix to evaluate designs where some criteria matter more than others — e.g. safety-critical criteria are non-negotiable, others are preferences
Include a user in the evaluation — explain each design to a peer acting as the user and record their responses as part of the evaluation

response_modes.reason: Students commonly select a preferred design based on personal preference and then justify it post-hoc rather than genuinely evaluating against criteria. The reasoning scaffold — apply criterion 1 to idea A and idea B, apply criterion 2, then decide — prevents preference-then-justify errors.

success_criteria: References the design criteria and user stories when selecting a preferred design
Gives at least one criterion-based reason for the preference
nodes.hinge_reason: Criterion-based evaluation in N2 is prerequisite for N3's modification task — students who evaluate by preference rather than criteria cannot identify which criterion is unmet, so N3's 'modify to address the gap' has no gap to address.

nodes.label: Modifying a design to meet unmet criteria
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify where a preferred design does not satisfy a criterion or user story and propose a modification to address it
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one gap between the preferred design and the design criteria; describe a modification that would address the gap
nodes.typical_width: Review the preferred design against all criteria and user stories; document which criteria are met and which are not; propose modifications for unmet criteria and explain how each modification addresses the gap
wider: Modify a game or game controller design so it can be used by a wider range of players — documenting what the original design assumed about the user and how the modification removes that assumption
Prototype a modification and evaluate whether it resolves the gap — going through one iteration of the design-modify-evaluate cycle

response_modes.reason: Students tend to treat modification as correcting errors rather than genuinely extending the design to meet unmet criteria. Contexts where the unmet criterion is clear and consequential — a game that only some students can play, an interface that only English readers can navigate — make the modification purpose concrete.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one gap between the preferred design and the criteria
Describes a modification that would address the identified gap
